name: Roman Baths
label: Roman Baths
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/500279537: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Roman Baths' (91 m across).
notes: Ancient Roman bathing complex and the Great Bath.

text.description:
The Roman Baths are a well-preserved Roman bathing complex in the middle of Bath. A temple was built here between 60 and 70 AD, and the Roman town of Aquae Sulis grew up around it. The hot spring still rises on the site. The water comes from rain that has soaked deep into the limestone of the Mendip Hills and been heated underground.

For a photographer, the appeal is the contrast between the Roman remains and the grand building around them. The buildings at street level are mostly 19th century. The visitor entrance is an 1897 concert hall with a glass-domed centre and a curved corner. Next to it is the Grand Pump Room, finished in 1799, whose front on Abbey Church Yard has four Corinthian columns and a pediment. This front is the easiest shot from outside, and the stone looks warm and even in good light.

Stand back far enough to fit the whole front, then move in for details such as the columns and the curve of the dome. Inside, you can tour the baths and museum, but you cannot enter the water. Check the official site before you go for entry arrangements and for any rules on photography indoors.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bath, Somerset, on Abbey Church Yard beside the Grand Pump Room. A bridge of the museum and Queen's Bath building spans York Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Bath and walk to Abbey Church Yard, where the Grand Pump Room and the visitor entrance stand side by side. No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so finish on foot in the city centre. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole front when you are close. Use the default lens (1x) for the general view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the columns, pediment and dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back a little along Abbey Church Yard to take in the Grand Pump Room front and the entrance building together.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the columns upright against the vertical lines. Try one wide shot of the whole front, then a tighter one of the Corinthian columns and pediment. If people are walking past, wait a moment for a clear gap.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone front to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the detail in the stonework is kept. Indoors, where it is dimmer, hold the phone steady with both hands and let night mode work if it switches on.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning or later in the afternoon, when there are usually fewer people in front of the building.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The area in front of the building is usually busiest in the middle of the day, so early morning or late afternoon is likely to be quieter.
The stone front tends to look warm and even in good daylight.
Interiors are usually dimmer than outdoors, so night mode may help.
Photography rules inside can vary, so they should be checked on the official site.
Walking time: 8 m x 1.3 / 80 m per minute is well under a minute, rounded up to about 1 minute.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 3 m from the phone icon

name: Thermae Bath Spa
label: Thermae Bath Spa
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/572837705: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Thermae Bath Spa' (60 m across).
notes: Modern spa with a rooftop pool overlooking the city.

text.description: Thermae Bath Spa is where Bath's old spa tradition meets a very modern building. The main block, the New Royal Bath, is a glass-enclosed cube built in Bath stone and designed by Grimshaw Architects. It sits among Georgian streets and neighbours the Georgian Cross Bath, which is grade I listed. That contrast between clean glass and honey-coloured historic stone is what makes it such a good subject for a phone. The spa reopened in 2006, ending a 28-year period when bathing in the city's hot spring water was not allowed. The water comes from the only naturally hot, mineral-rich springs in the UK, and the council has been its guardian under a royal charter of 1590. Inside the glass cube there is an open-air rooftop pool, though the pools themselves are for paying spa guests, so for most visitors the photo is of the building from the street. Look for reflections in the glass, where the older buildings nearby show up as softer shapes. Step back a little to fit the whole cube in, then try a second shot closer in, aiming at the meeting point of the stone and the glass. Keep the phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. Please be considerate of spa guests, and do not photograph people inside or on the rooftop.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bath, in the Georgian streets of the old spa quarter, close to the historic Hot Bath and Cross Bath buildings.
text.directions_text: There are no train or bus stops listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Bath and head for the spa quarter, close to the Cross Bath. The phone icon on the map marks the centre of the spa building, so use it as your reference and shoot from the public area around it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole glass cube. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too narrow to step back. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for details of the glass and stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Choose a place on the nearby public street from where the whole cube fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the cube with the vertical lines so the walls do not lean. Include a slice of the Georgian stone buildings beside it to show the contrast between old and new. For a second shot, go close with 2x and frame the join between glass and Bath stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or the glass is washing out. Ultra-wide shots from close up can bend vertical lines, so keep the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to the stone, and glass reflections are often clearest on bright but not harsh days. At dusk the lit-up interior can glow against the darkening sky, so try night mode, holding the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The streets around the building are public, but the spa itself is a paid, bookable attraction, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Bath Abbey
label: Bath Abbey
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Abbey Churchyard' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Abbey Churchyard' (way/39675782): middle (82 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39333604: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bath Abbey' (85 m across).
notes: Late medieval abbey church with a famous west front.

text.description:
Bath Abbey is the great Gothic church at the heart of the city, and its west front is the view most visitors want. The west front has sculptures of angels climbing two stone ladders, representing Jacob's Ladder, which make a lovely detail to look for. The church was founded in the 7th century, rebuilt in the 12th and 16th centuries, and restored by Sir George Gilbert Scott in the 1860s. It is a fine example of Perpendicular Gothic, which means tall windows and strong vertical lines. Inside it is famous for its fan vaulting, and it is still an active place of worship that seats up to 1,200 people.

The building photographs well because the open square in front gives you room to see the whole façade in one frame. A few people or a street performer in the foreground add life and give a sense of scale. The square can get busy, so be patient and wait for a gap. For a quieter shot, try the York Street archway for a tighter, more detailed frame, or Church Street for a slightly wider view with the small fudge shop in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: Bath Abbey stands in the centre of Bath.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Bath city centre and head for the Abbey in the centre of Bath, asking for Abbey Churchyard if you need to. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the west front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you cannot step back far enough to fit the whole façade in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved angels on the ladders and the window tracery.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Abbey Churchyard (in front of the Abbey's main west entrance). The full Gothic west front of the Abbey, framed by the open square, with the option of adding people or street performers in the foreground. This gives the classic straight-on view of the full Gothic west front, framed by the open square. The Abbey is to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the towers with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep your phone upright and level, and avoid tilting it up, which makes the walls lean inwards. Let a few people or a street performer into the lower part of the frame for life and scale. For a tighter, more detailed shot, try the York Street archway. For a slightly wider view with the fudge shop in the foreground, try Church Street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale sky does not wash out the detail. If people walk through your shot, take a Live Photo or a quick burst and pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning for fewer people in the square. The west front is likely to catch the light in the afternoon and evening.

text.access_note: The square in front of the Abbey is open public space, but the Abbey itself is an active place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any dress or behaviour guidance.
claims_not_in_sources: The square can be busy with crowds and street performers, and early morning is likely to be quieter.
The west front is likely to catch the afternoon and evening light because it faces west.
Standing close and tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings look as if they lean inwards.
The York Street archway and Church Street are quieter alternative viewpoints near the Abbey.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 54 m from the phone icon

name: Royal Crescent
label: Royal Crescent
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Royal Victoria Park' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Royal Victoria Park' (way/444067360): edge nearest the subject (1146 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/121115396: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (23 m across).
notes: Sweeping Georgian crescent of 30 terraced houses.

text.description:
The Royal Crescent is a sweeping row of 30 Georgian townhouses in Bath. John Wood the Younger designed it, and it was built between 1767 and 1774. It is Grade I listed, and the stone front still looks much as it did when it was new. The curve is about 150 metres long, with 114 tall Ionic columns running along the first floor, so the whole terrace has a calm, even rhythm.

It photographs well because of the setting. The houses face open parkland, and a ha-ha (a sunken, stone-faced ditch) divides the lawns without blocking the view from Royal Victoria Park. That leaves a clean green foreground below the honey-coloured stone. The usual way to see the whole curve is from the lawn of Royal Victoria Park, a little way back from the ha-ha.

For your phone, the aim is to show the full arc with some grass in front. Stand back far enough that both ends of the terrace fit, keep the phone level so the rooflines stay straight, and use the gridlines to line up the columns. If you want a quieter angle with fewer people and parked cars, try Marlborough Buildings. Brock Street is another good option, as it frames the Crescent with the lawn and trees. Whichever you pick, take a wide shot first, then a closer one of the columns and the ha-ha.
text.geographic_location: The Royal Crescent is in the city of Bath, on the edge of Royal Victoria Park, and is linked by Brock Street to The Circus.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed for this spot, so start from The Circus in Bath and walk along Brock Street to the Crescent. Then walk onto the public park lawn facing the terrace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can only stand fairly close, then try the default lens (1x) from further back for straighter, more natural edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x) for details such as the columns, the lamp posts or the front doors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Royal Victoria Park (lawn directly in front of the Crescent, beyond the ha-ha). The whole sweeping curve of the terrace with the green lawn in the foreground. At that distance you will not fit the whole 150-metre curve, so step back south across the lawn, staying on the public park side, until both ends of the terrace are in view with green grass in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Step back until both ends of the curve are in the frame, and keep the phone level so the rooflines don't lean. Let the lawn fill the bottom third of the picture. Use the gridlines to keep the columns upright. For a different view, try Brock Street, where the Crescent sits against the lawn and trees, or Marlborough Buildings for a quieter angle with fewer people and parked cars.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Turn on gridlines. Tap the stone facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. Panorama can work if you hold the phone very steady, but a single ultra-wide shot is easier.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the Bath stone looks warm and golden.

text.access_note: The park lawn is public open land, but the grass directly in front of the houses may be for residents only, so stay on the park side of the ha-ha; for No. 1 Royal Crescent museum or the hotel, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: An ultra-wide (0.5x) lens helps fit the whole curve in when you stand fairly close.
Early morning and late afternoon light makes the stone look warm and golden.

name: Pulteney Bridge
label: Pulteney Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Grand Parade' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Grand Parade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/369771678: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Pulteney Bridge' (58 m across).
notes: Georgian bridge lined with shops over the River Avon.

text.description: Pulteney Bridge carries a street of small shops across the River Avon, and it is one of the most photographed sights in Bath. Robert Adam designed it in a Palladian style, and it was finished by 1774 to link the city with new building land on the Bathwick side. Only four bridges in the world have shops along the full length of both sides, and this is one of them. It is now Grade I listed. The pale limestone south face, with its three arches and temple-like central section, is the side that still shows Adam's hand. The north side has been altered over the years. Below the bridge, the river drops over a weir, which gives your photo a good foreground. From here you can fit the three arches, the weir and the green hills behind the city into one frame. This is the classic daytime view. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, because the bridge looks quite different wide and close. Buses and taxis still use the bridge, so keep clear of the roadway if you walk across for shots of the shopfronts. Works around the weir happen from time to time, so the foreground may not always look the same.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bath, where the bridge crosses the River Avon between the old city and the Bathwick side. Grand Parade runs along the river just to the south-west of it.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Bath, walk down to Grand Parade by the river. Once you are by the river, the bridge is easy to spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge and weir together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or railings crowd your view. Use telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) for the arches and the Palladian detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Grand Parade (Elevated position on the east side above the river, looking down toward the bridge). The bridge's three arches and the weir below, with green hills rising behind the city. This is the view guides name as the best of the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge on one of the lower lines, with the weir and the hills filling the rest of the frame. Keep the phone level so the arches don't lean. For a lower, closer view with the weir in the foreground, try Parade Gardens (check before you go whether there is a charge). You can also take a different angle from North Parade Bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the limestone keeps its detail. A Live Photo can catch the movement of the water over the weir.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime is the classic time for the bridge and weir together. For a view of the bridge lit up in the evening, try North Parade Bridge.

text.access_note: Grand Parade is a public street, but check on the day whether there is a charge for Parade Gardens.

name: Jane Austen Centre
label: Jane Austen Centre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen Square' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Queen Square' (way/59967625): middle (106 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/557083339: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jane Austen Centre' (15 m across).
notes: Museum on Gay Street dedicated to the author.

text.description:
The Jane Austen Centre is at 40 Gay Street, in a terrace of Georgian townhouses a short walk north-east of the top right corner of Queen Square. Inside, a permanent exhibition tells the story of Jane Austen's time in Bath and how living in the city shaped her writing. There are also Regency Tea Rooms, and a life-size wax figure of the author that was unveiled in 2014. The Centre also hosts the annual Jane Austen Festival, which has run since 2001.

For a phone photographer, the building works best as part of its street. The Centre sits in a block (31–40 Gay Street) that is Grade II listed, so the straight, even townhouse frontage gives you strong lines to work with. The best lead-in is the top right corner of Queen Square, where Gay Street leads off. From here you can take a wider shot of the approach up the street, with the Centre's frontage at the far end. It is a calmer view than a close-up at the door, and it keeps the terrace in the picture.

If you want the detail instead, walk up to the Centre itself. The front shows the entrance, a floral display and the statue or costumed figure of Jane Austen on the porch. That figure may be moved or absent on some days, so check the frontage when you arrive. Gay Street is narrow and busy, so look around before you step back to frame a shot.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bath, on Gay Street, a short step north-east of Queen Square among the Georgian terraces.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops listed nearby, so head for Queen Square in the centre of Bath. From there the Centre is about 1 minute on foot to the north-east, up Gay Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the street and the full townhouse terrace. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the frontage closer without walking into the traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Queen Square (top right corner of the square, where Gay Street leads off). A wider shot of the approach up Gay Street, with the Centre's townhouse frontage at the far end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the street up with the vertical lines so the terrace doesn't lean. Let the buildings on both sides lead the eye towards the Centre. For a close-up of the entrance, floral display and Jane Austen figure on the porch, walk up to the Centre's front, but watch for passing people and traffic when you step back.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Centre's frontage to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on a narrow street like this.

text.access_note: The street and Queen Square are open public space, but the Centre itself is a ticketed attraction that recommends pre-booking, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is likely to be quieter on Gay Street.
Slightly lowering the exposure helps keep detail in stonework when the sky is bright.

name: The Circus
label: The Circus
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Alexandra Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Alexandra Park' (way/3027363): middle (352 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/676607666: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '' (23 m across).
notes: Circular Georgian street of townhouses by John Wood the Elder.

text.description: The Circus is a ring of large Georgian townhouses, built between 1754 and 1768 and designed by John Wood the Elder. It is Grade I listed. Wood made the ring 318 feet (97 m) across, echoing the size of Stonehenge. He died soon after the first stone was laid, and his son, John Wood the Younger, finished it. The curved façades stack three classical styles one above the other, and the frieze carries 525 small carved emblems. In the middle is a lawn with five large plane trees. The Circus sits in the same frame as the Abbey and the Royal Crescent, so it makes a good 'where does it all fit?' picture. Be realistic about it: from up here the Circus is one small part of the scene, not the subject. The benches on the high ground in the north-east corner give the best outlook, and it is worth checking the exact spot when you arrive. If you want the full circular sweep of the three curved terraces, with the trees framing the ring of houses, go down to The Circus itself and shoot from the street. Together the two pictures make a nice pair.
text.geographic_location: The Circus is in the Georgian part of Bath, close to Queen Square and Gay Street.
text.directions_text: Start from Bath city centre and head to Alexandra Park, then go to the benches on the high ground in the north-east corner. From there The Circus lies to the north, about 1.3 km away in a straight line. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole panorama. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring The Circus and the Royal Crescent closer. If you go down to The Circus itself, the ultra-wide (0.5x) helps fit in the curve of the terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Alexandra Park (north-east corner, bench cluster on the high ground). A panoramic view over the Georgian city centre, where The Circus sits in the same frame as the Abbey and the Royal Crescent.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper line so the rooftops and the city fill the frame. Let the Abbey and the crescents spread across the frame, and use the park's trees or the bench edge in the foreground to add depth. For a closer view of the ring of houses with the central trees, use The Circus itself as a second viewpoint.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the city to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. At 2x or more, hold the phone steady with both hands, or rest your elbows on a bench back.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning for clear air, or late afternoon for light on the crescents.

text.access_note: Alexandra Park is a public park; The Circus is a ring of houses with a lawn in the middle, so check whether the lawn is open to walk on at the time of your visit.
claims_not_in_sources: Alexandra Park lies on high ground south of Bath city centre.
The Circus is a ring of residential houses with a public street around it.
Gridlines and exposure sliders are available in the default camera app on most smartphones.
Holding a phone steady at 2x zoom or more helps keep telephoto shots sharp.

name: Holburne Museum
label: Holburne Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Laura Place' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Laura Place' (way/683648842): middle (14 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/40034967: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Holburne Museum' (160 m across).
notes: Art museum at the end of Great Pulteney Street.

text.description:
The Holburne Museum is a handsome Grade I listed building standing at the far end of Great Pulteney Street, with Sydney Gardens behind it. It was built as the Sydney Hotel, with the foundation stone laid in 1796, to serve the pleasure gardens. It has been a museum since 1916 and was Bath's first public art gallery. A modern extension by Eric Parry Architects, with ceramic cladding, opened in 2011 and sits at the rear.

A recommended long view is from Laura Place, by the fountain. From there Great Pulteney Street runs straight away from you and the museum closes the view at the far end. It is only a small part of the building in the distance, so treat it as a wide, scene-setting shot: the long street does the work and the museum is the destination. For a closer look at the historic front, Sydney Road beside Sydney Gardens is worth trying. The modern glass extension, with its dark blue ceramic fins, can be framed by trees from inside Sydney Gardens. Exact standing points for those two views are best found on the ground.

Keep the street lines straight and let them lead the eye to the building. Wait for a gap in passing people and traffic if you can. If you want the museum larger in the frame, use your phone's zoom rather than walking into the road.
text.geographic_location: The museum stands in Sydney Gardens at the end of Great Pulteney Street, in the north-east part of central Bath. Laura Place, where the long view begins, is at the other end of that street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed nearby. Laura Place is in central Bath, so head there first. It is about 450 m, a short walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full street view, then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the museum closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) will make the museum look very small at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Laura Place (by the fountain, looking down Great Pulteney Street). Great Pulteney Street running straight ahead, with the Holburne Museum visible at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the street's centre line in the middle of the frame so the buildings on both sides lead towards the museum. Include a little foreground, such as the fountain, to give a sense of depth. If you also want the museum's front or its modern extension, Sydney Road and Sydney Gardens offer those views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the museum to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright. Keep the phone level so the street's edges stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is likely to be quieter, with fewer people and cars in the street. Choose a time when light falls on the street's buildings rather than straight into your lens.

text.access_note: Laura Place and Great Pulteney Street are public streets, but the museum itself is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry details.

name: Bath Spa railway station
label: Bath Spa station
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Dorchester Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Dorchester Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/6605149668: the OpenStreetMap point 'Bath Spa'.

text.description:
Bath Spa is the city's main railway station, and for many visitors it is the first building they see. Isambard Kingdom Brunel designed it for the Great Western Railway, and it opened on 31 August 1840. It is a Grade II* listed building in an asymmetrical Tudor style, with curving gables. That mix of shapes and stonework gives you plenty to frame, even on a short stop between trains.

The best everyday view is from Dorchester Street, outside the frontage. Stand in the street and look towards the main entrance, and the street itself frames the building. The gabled front fills the picture well, and you can include a little of the surroundings to show it is a working station. One detail is worth knowing: the clock above the main entrance was taken down in 2022 because of safety concerns about the Dutch gable, and as of April 2026 it had not been put back. So you may see a gap where you might expect a clock.

If you have the energy for a different view, Beechen Cliff looks down over the station and the city on the wooded hillside. It is a steep climb, so allow time. Bring the phone zoom to pick out the station from that distance.

Back at street level, keep an eye on passers-by and vehicles, and take a few frames so you can choose the cleanest one later.
text.geographic_location: Bath Spa station sits on the north bank of the River Avon, on the edge of the city centre. The Royal Station Hotel is next to it, and a footbridge at the back of the station leads across the river to Widcombe.
text.directions_text: If you arrive by train, you are already here: walk out of the main entrance to the street frontage. From Widcombe, cross the footbridge over the Avon at the back of the station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the frontage. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough, and keep the building well away from the edges of the frame so it does not look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Dorchester Street (looking east toward the main station entrance, from the street outside the frontage). The Tudor-style Brunel-era station frontage and entrance, framed by the street. Look towards the main station entrance, which is to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the gables and the building's edges with them, so the verticals stay straight. Hold the phone level and a little above chest height. Include some of the street in the lower part of the picture to give a sense of arriving. For a different view, Beechen Cliff looks down over the station and the city. It is a steep climb, so use the zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Take a few frames in case people or vehicles pass through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime, when the stonework is evenly lit. Early morning is usually the quietest time for people in front of the building.

text.access_note: The frontage can be photographed from the public street, but this is a working railway station with ticket barriers, so check the official site before you go if you want to photograph on the platforms.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter outside the station frontage.
Even daytime light suits the stonework and helps the building keep its detail.
Vehicles and pedestrians are likely to pass in front of the frontage on Dorchester Street.
Photographing on the platforms may need a ticket or permission.

name: Royal Victoria Park
label: Royal Victoria Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bath Botanical Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Botanical Gardens' (way/47005215): middle (271 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/444067360: large area 'Royal Victoria Park' (1146 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Large Georgian park below the Royal Crescent.

text.description: Royal Victoria Park is Bath's big public park, spread out below the Royal Crescent. It was opened in 1830 by the 11-year-old Princess Victoria, seven years before she became queen, and it was the first park to carry her name. Today it covers about 57 acres (23 ha), with lawns, tall trees and play areas. It is also Grade I registered for its historic importance. For photos, the Bath Botanical Gardens in the north-west corner are an easy place to start. They were laid out in 1887 and hold a fine collection of plants that grow on limestone. You get flower beds, trees and plant displays, with colour in spring, summer and autumn. A photography guide rates the gardens for nature pictures and says autumn is as good as the flowering months. If you walk further into the park, the Georgian crescent curves out from behind the trees, which makes a classic view across the lawns. Near the east entrance on Marlborough Lane stands the Victoria Column, a stone obelisk about 10 m tall put up in 1837. It makes a neat second subject if you have time. Keep your phone steady, look for a foreground of flowers or leaves, and leave plenty of lawn or sky around the Crescent so the picture feels open.
text.geographic_location: Royal Victoria Park is in Bath, just below the Royal Crescent. The Botanical Gardens are in its north-west corner.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Bath, head to the Royal Crescent on foot; the park lies just below it. The Botanical Gardens are entered from the Crescent side of the park, in its north-west corner. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for flower beds and tree-lined paths. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for wide lawns and sweeping views. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single bloom or to bring the Crescent closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Bath Botanical Gardens (north-west corner of Royal Victoria Park, entered from the Crescent side). Flower beds, trees and plant displays, with seasonal colour in spring, summer and autumn. From here you can photograph the flower beds, trees and plant displays, with the wider park opening out to the south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use gridlines and place a bed of flowers or a curving path in the lower third, with trees behind. For the wider park, an alternative is to walk out onto the lawns and look north, so the Georgian crescent curves out from behind the trees, framed by foliage.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the flowers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich and bright petals do not wash out. Portrait mode can blur the background behind a single plant.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Spring, summer and autumn all bring colour, and autumn is described as just as good as the flowering months. Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kind to flowers and leaves.

text.access_note: Royal Victoria Park is a public park, but gardens and events can affect access, so check the official site for current access and any closures before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The Royal Crescent lies on the northern edge of the park, so views of it from the lawns look north.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light is kinder for photographing flowers and leaves than harsh midday sun.
The walk from the stand-here point to the middle of the park takes roughly six minutes.

name: Parade Gardens
label: Parade Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parade Gardens' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parade Gardens' (way/3027776): middle (204 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/3027776: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parade Gardens' (205 m across).
notes: Riverside gardens beside the Avon with views of the abbey.

text.description: Parade Gardens is a grade II listed park in the centre of Bath, set beside the River Avon. It was laid out in 1709 and was first called St James's Park, made for visitors who came to take the waters. After the Bath Royal Literary and Scientific Institution was built in 1824, it became known as the Institution Gardens for a time. For a phone photo, the appeal is the layered view: flower beds and lawns in the foreground, then the river, the weir and Pulteney Bridge behind. The colonnade along the western edge is the spot guides recommend for this view, and it is a popular place for photos. It also gives you a little shade and a frame of columns if you want one. Take a wide shot first, then move in on details such as a bed of flowers with the weir softly behind. If you want a different angle, North Parade Bridge gives a higher, wider view down onto the gardens, with the river and Pulteney Bridge beyond. The gardens are about 250 yards east of Bath Abbey, so they fit easily into a walk round the centre. There is a cafe on site. Entry arrangements have changed over time, so check the official site before you go. Keep your phone steady against a column or the railing for sharper shots.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Bath, south of the Empire Hotel and about 250 yards east of Bath Abbey, beside the River Avon.
text.directions_text: Start from Bath Abbey and head east; the gardens are about 250 yards away. Once inside, go to the colonnade along the western edge and stand. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full view of beds, river and bridge. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the colonnade and more of the lawns. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the weir or Pulteney Bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parade Gardens (western boundary colonnade, looking across the gardens toward the river). The flower beds and lawns in the foreground with the River Avon, the weir and Pulteney Bridge behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the river on the upper third line, with the flower beds filling the lower part. Use a column of the colonnade at the edge of the picture as a frame. For a higher, wider view down onto the gardens, try North Parade Bridge instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the flower beds to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. Try panorama for the sweep of river and bridge, and hold the phone level as you pan.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light, and the flower beds look best in the warmer months.

text.access_note: Entry arrangements have changed over time and may involve a fee, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light for photos.
The flower beds look best in the warmer months.
The colonnade can give some shade and a natural frame for photos.

name: Bath Assembly Rooms
label: Assembly Rooms
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bennett Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bennett Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4524730: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Assembly Rooms' (82 m across).
notes: Georgian public rooms for fashionable society.

text.description:
The Assembly Rooms are a Georgian social venue in Bath, designed by John Wood the Younger in 1769 and opened with a grand ball in 1771. Jane Austen and Charles Dickens both knew them, and Austen mentions them in Northanger Abbey and Persuasion. The building is made of Bath stone and laid out in a U shape. Its ballroom is about 30 metres long, the largest Georgian interior in Bath. It was bombed and burnt out in the Second World War, then restored and reopened in 1963. It is now a Grade I listed building owned by the National Trust.

For a phone photo, the best subject is the outside. From Bennett Street you see the colonnaded front head-on, with its row of columns and arched windows, in the warm, creamy stone that Bath is known for. The straight-on view suits gridlines well, because the columns and windows repeat in clean lines. If you have time, Alfred Street gives a different angle on the side of the building, with its tall windows and chimneystacks.

The National Trust says the building is under renovation, so hoardings may partly screen the front. Check the official site before you go to see how much is visible. Keep an eye on traffic and other pedestrians on the street while you line up your shot.
text.geographic_location: The Assembly Rooms stand in Bath's Georgian area between Queen Square, The Circus and the Royal Crescent; the viewpoint is on Bennett Street.
text.directions_text: Head for the Georgian area between Queen Square, The Circus and the Royal Crescent, and look for Bennett Street. Navigate to the Assembly Rooms on Bennett Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the columns and windows keep a natural shape. If the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the whole front in, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) and keep the phone level. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close shots of the columns and arched windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bennett Street (opposite the colonnaded north front, by the Ballroom). The colonnaded Bath stone front of the Assembly Rooms, with its columns and arched windows, seen straight on from the street. For a second angle, walk round to Alfred Street and shoot the side of the building at an angle, with its tall windows and chimneystacks.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the row of columns with the vertical lines so the front looks straight. Stand square to the middle of the front and keep the phone upright to avoid leaning walls. If hoardings or scaffolding cover part of the front, move in on a section that is clear, such as a group of columns and windows. Alfred Street is a good alternative for a side-on view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building's stone to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour and detail. Do not use portrait mode for the building itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Bright overcast daylight or a clear morning should give even light on the stone. Early in the day there are also usually fewer people on the pavement.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside from the public street, but the building is a National Trust visitor attraction under renovation, so check the official site before you go for access and what is visible.
claims_not_in_sources: A north-facing front gets little direct sun, so even, bright overcast light is likely to suit it.
Early in the day there are usually fewer people on the pavement.
Traffic and other pedestrians may be present on Bennett Street.

name: Queen Square
label: Queen Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Queen Square Place' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Queen Square and Queen Square Place (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/59967625: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Queen Square' (106 m across).
notes: Georgian square designed by John Wood the Elder.

text.description:
Queen Square is a square of Georgian houses on the edge of Bath's old centre. It is the first piece of John Wood the Elder's grand scheme, which carries on north to the Circus and the Royal Crescent. Every building around it is Grade I listed. Wood designed the fronts to look like a palace, and the north side is the showpiece: seven separate houses that read as one grand frontage. In the middle of the garden stands an obelisk put up by Beau Nash in 1738 for Frederick, Prince of Wales. It was once taller, until a gale in 1815 cut it short.

For a phone photo, the square works because it is neat and symmetrical: pale stone terraces, tall trees and a clear centre line. The garden has mature trees, so leaves can block the obelisk in summer. Boules tournaments, the July food festival marquees and lunchtime office crowds can also get in the way. Take a few frames, then step a little to either side to find a gap that keeps the terrace roofline clean.
text.geographic_location: Queen Square is in the Georgian part of central Bath, just outside the line of the old medieval city walls. It lies south of Gay Street, which leads up to the Circus and the Royal Crescent.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Abbey and Pump Room area in the centre of Bath. Queen Square is a short walk from there. Once you are at the square, find the corner where Queen Square Place meets it. From there the middle of the square is about 20 m to the east, a few seconds' walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole terrace and the trees in one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a tidier view. Use telephoto (2x-3x, or up to 5x on some phones) to pick out the doorways and rooflines of one terrace.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Queen Square and Queen Square Place (corner where Queen Square Place meets the square). A framed view across the square, of the Georgian terraces on the far side.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the terrace rooflines up with the top third of the frame so the buildings look straight. Let the trees and the garden railings form a natural frame on the near side. If you want the obelisk too, take a second shot from the square itself with the terraces behind it. Its centre point also suits a wide shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the stonework keep their detail. If people walk through the frame, take a short burst or a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day on a weekday is likely to be calmest, before the lunchtime office crowds, and the low sun on the stone is flattering. Avoid event days if you want a clear view across the garden.

text.access_note: Queen Square hosts markets and events, so check access and the official site before you go if you are planning around an event.

name: Great Pulteney Street
label: Great Pulteney St
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Laura Place' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Laura Place' (way/683648842): middle (14 m across).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5599814: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Wide Georgian boulevard leading to the Holburne Museum.

text.description: Great Pulteney Street is a wide, straight Georgian avenue that runs from Pulteney Bridge across the River Avon towards the Holburne Museum, which closes the far end. It was designed by Thomas Baldwin and finished in 1789. It is over 300 m long and about 30 m wide, which makes it the widest and grandest street in Bath. Baldwin designed only the façades. Individual owners built the houses behind them, so the street looks uniform from outside but differs inside. This is why it photographs so well: the rows of matching windows, doors and steps lead the eye down the street in clean lines, and the end of the street is clearly closed by a building. Look closely and you will find small differences, such as door heights, balconies and the painted house numbers. The numbering skips number 13. The best overall view is from Laura Place, the small square at the city end, beside the fountain. The fountain replaced a much grander column that local residents began and then abandoned, because it would have towered over the houses. For a different angle, try the view straight down the avenue from Pulteney Bridge, or the museum's frontage at the far end. Keep your horizon level and wait for a gap in the people and traffic.
text.geographic_location: Great Pulteney Street is in Bathwick, on the east side of the River Avon, just across Pulteney Bridge from the city centre. Laura Place, the viewpoint, sits at the bridge end of the street.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Bath and walk over Pulteney Bridge towards Bathwick. Laura Place is the square at the city end of the street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full width of the street and the façades on both sides. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it to pull the Holburne Museum closer at the end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Laura Place (by the fountain at the centre of the square, looking along the street). The full length of Great Pulteney Street running away from the fountain toward the Holburne Museum, with its Georgian facades lining both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the centre of the road with the middle of the frame, so the two rows of houses converge evenly. Keep the phone upright and level so the buildings do not lean. For a second view, try the straight view down the avenue from Pulteney Bridge, or the museum's frontage at the far end of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the houses in the middle distance to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its detail. Take a few frames, as traffic and passers-by change from shot to shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon tends to give softer light on the stone and fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The street and Laura Place are open public spaces; the Holburne Museum is a visitor attraction, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: Kennet and Avon Canal at Bath Locks
label: Bath Locks canal
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3577624: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Canal locks on the Kennet and Avon Canal towpath.

text.description: Bath Locks mark the start of the Kennet and Avon Canal, where it climbs away from the River Avon in the middle of the city. There are now six locks in a short run, which gives you stepped water, lock gates and walkways in one view. The Bottom Lock sits just south of Pulteney Bridge, and the canal then rises through the Deep Lock, Wash House Lock, Abbey View Lock, Pulteney Lock and the Top Lock. The Deep Lock is the one to look for. Its chamber is 5.92 metres deep, which makes it Britain's second deepest canal lock, and it was created in 1976 when two locks were combined during the canal's restoration. Abbey View Lock is a Grade II listed structure. The locks themselves were restored in 1968 by British Waterways staff working with volunteers from the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust. For a phone photo, the appeal is the repeating lines of the gates and the water stepping uphill. Look for a frame where the lock edge or a gate beam leads the eye towards the next lock. People walking the towpath or a boat in a lock give a sense of scale, but wait for a gap if you want a clean shot of the water. Keep the phone steady against a rail or your body, and check the edges of the frame for stray bins and signs.
text.geographic_location: In Bath, at the start of the Kennet and Avon Canal, a short way south of Pulteney Bridge and below Sydney Gardens.
text.directions_text: Start from the Pulteney Bridge area in central Bath, which is well known and easy to find, and walk to the canal. From there the locks are about 171 m to the east, which is about 3 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the lock and the water together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you get close to the Deep Lock and want its depth and the gates in one frame. The telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out a single gate or a boat from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Zoom in to 2x or 3x from here, or walk the few minutes along the canal for a closer, wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a lock edge or the towpath up with one of them so the stepped locks lead the eye into the picture. Include a lock gate in the foreground for depth. If a boat or a walker passes through, wait for them to be in the right place in the frame. Keep your distance from the edge of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or a lock gate to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky or the water is bright, so the detail in the gates and stonework stays.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Light in the middle of a bright day can cause glare on the water, and the towpath may be busier then.

text.access_note: The locks are by the canal towpath in the city, but check the official site (for example Canal & River Trust) before you go in case of closures or works.
claims_not_in_sources: The Pulteney Bridge area is well known and a sensible starting point.
The towpath beside the locks is generally open to walkers.
The towpath may be closed occasionally for works or maintenance.
Light is softer early and late in the day, and glare on water is stronger at midday.
The towpath may be busier in the middle of the day.
Boats and walkers pass through the locks.
There are rails, bins and signs near the locks that could appear in photos.
